desc:
A non-empty string is a Lyndon word if it is strictly smaller (in dictionary order) than each of its proper suffixes. For example "ab", "aab" and "a" are Lyndon words, while "ba", "aa" and "abab" are not.

Every string s can be written in exactly one way as a concatenation w1 w2 ... wk of Lyndon words with w1 ≥ w2 ≥ ... ≥ wk (dictionary order, equal neighbours allowed). Return the lengths |w1|, ..., |wk| in order.

Example: s = "banana" factorizes as b | an | an | a, so the answer is [1, 2, 2, 1]. For s = "abab" the factors are ab | ab and the answer is [2, 2].
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: The first factor w1 is the longest prefix of s that is a Lyndon word. Testing every prefix naively is too slow, so think about growing a prefix and keeping its structure.

Duval's algorithm keeps a pointer i (start of the unfinished part), a position j being examined and a pointer k = j - period. While s[k] <= s[j] the prefix s[i..j] is still (a power of a Lyndon word) plus a prefix of it.

If s[k] < s[j], the whole block becomes one Lyndon word, so reset k = i; if equal, advance k. When the loop stops, emit the repeated Lyndon word of length j - k as many times as it fits starting from i, then restart from the first position not yet emitted.
editorial: Duval's algorithm. Let the current unprocessed part start at i. Scan with j = i + 1 and k = i, where the invariant is that s[i..j-1] is of the form umu' with u a Lyndon word of length j - k and u' a proper prefix of u.

While j < n and s[k] ≤ s[j]: if s[k] < s[j] the extended string is itself a Lyndon word (the period becomes the whole length), so k = i; otherwise (equal) just k += 1; then j += 1. When the loop stops, the factor length is L = j - k. Output L repeatedly while i ≤ k, advancing i by L each time; the leftover u' is processed again from the new i.
Each character is re-examined only a bounded number of times: at most twice overall, so the total running time is O(n) and the extra space is O(1) besides the output.
solution:
def lyndonFactors(s):
    n = len(s)
    i = 0
    out = []
    while i < n:
        j, k = i + 1, i
        while j < n and s[k] <= s[j]:
            k = i if s[k] < s[j] else k + 1
            j += 1
        L = j - k
        while i <= k:
            out.append(L)
            i += L
    return out
